🇲🇽🇺🇸 <u>"Cooperation always, subordination never": Sheinbaum draws the line with the US</u>

From Monterrey, Sheinbaum told the neighbor to the north exactly where the border of dignity runs: "Cooperation always, subordination never — that is the essence of Mexicans." She wants a good relationship with Trump's Washington, but "cooperation does not mean submission; friendship does not mean renouncing our principles. While I am president, I will defend our sovereignty, our dignity and our independence with all firmness."

🇲🇽🇨🇳 <u>China backs Mexico's sovereignty against foreign interference</u>

While Washington threatens tariffs and floats "military options" against cartels, Beijing went the other way: meeting Foreign Minister Roberto Velasco, China's Wang Yi voiced support for "Mexico's independence and autonomy... and its opposition to foreign interference," stressing that China–Mexico ties "are not directed at third parties and should not be affected by third parties." Velasco announced a new Mexican consulate in Chongqing.

<u>US MEDIA — SILENCE</u>: Mexico's 581-km Mexico City–Guadalajara passenger train
September 6, 2026 | 🇲🇽

🇲🇽 Sheinbaum announced construction begins in 2027 on a 581-km passenger railway linking Mexico City to Guadalajara through five states — part of a national rail revival abandoned for a generation. US mainstream coverage: zero. 📰

The same outlets that cover every cartel bombing had nothing on a multi-year public infrastructure project crossing Hidalgo, Querétaro, Guanajuato and Jalisco.

• 581 km across 5 states; construction 2027, targeted completion 2029.
• Carried only by Mexican and solidarity outlets — no NYT, WaPo, AP or Reuters pickup.

<u>HSTODAY / US EMBASSY</u>: "US and Mexico Strengthen Cooperation to Disrupt Cartel Financial Networks"
September 7, 2026 | 🟡

📰 A US homeland-security outlet runs the US Embassy's cartel-finance press release as straight news — "cooperation advanced by President Trump and President Sheinbaum," with US Ambassador Ronald Johnson as the only named voice. 🔍

Mexico's own Financial Intelligence Unit does the tracking, sanctioning and seizing — but the story is narrated entirely from Washington's side of the table.

• "We follow the money and those who touch it are stained and will have no place to hide." — Amb. Johnson
• "If we take away the money that makes everything else possible, we catch them in the very heart of their criminal networks." — Amb. Johnson

<u>NEWSNATION</u>: Congressman says midshipman's mom deported back to Mexico
September 3, 2026 | 🟡

📰 ICE detained Maria Rocio Rocha at her USCIS green-card interview on Aug. 25, then deported her to Mexico this week. Her son, David Garcia, is a US Naval Academy midshipman. Her own congressman says she was "doing everything the right way." 💀

She was held at the Dilley, Texas detention center; ICE blocked Rep. Joaquin Castro from visiting and "did not immediately respond to requests for comment."

• "Maria should be home, not torn apart from her family and life." — Rep. Castro
• "We cannot allow the president's mass deportation campaign to destroy more families for profit."

🇲🇽🗳️ <u>Morena's mass base dwarfs the PAN in Mexico City</u>

The rolls tell the story of Mexico's realignment. Heading into 2027, Morena counts more than 1.1 million members in Mexico City alone, while the right-wing PAN crawled from about 18,000 to just 38,314 affiliates, according to INE-certified party registries. Nationally, 43% of Mexicans identify with Morena, per the latest Enkoll poll — as the PRI and Movimiento Ciudadano keep shrinking.

🚨🇲🇽 <u>Guerrero sweep: 71 armed "police" detained, 284 guns seized</u>

In a coordinated operation across Tlapa, Chilapa and Atlixtac, Guerrero's Operativo Enjambre detained 71 armed men working as "police" and seized 284 firearms. The 66 who proved they were accredited officers were released; five remain under investigation — among them Tlapa's transport director and three Chilapa officers accused of unlawful detention and abuse of authority. The state is auditing exactly who carries a badge and a gun in the Montaña.

🔥🇲🇽 <u>Purépecha to the government: rights mean land, not just recognition</u>

Purépecha communities in Michoacán are pushing back on the government's own Indigenous rights bill — not to reject rights, but to demand more. The Council of Indigenous Communities (CSIM) refuses to let the INPI speak for them and calls the draft "a setback" because it fails to guarantee territory, direct budgets, and community control over security, justice and water, including Lake Zirahuén. Self-determination, they insist, has to include the land.

🇲🇽📚 <u>Governments have always wanted the rural teacher colleges gone</u>

The normales rurales — where "the children of peasants, workers and low-income families study" — are still in the crosshairs. Specialist Hallier Morales tells La Jornada that federal and state governments "have always sought to disappear these schools, because they are spaces of resistance and organization, not only of students but of communities." Ayotzinapa is the most famous of them; eleven years after the 43, the pressure on rural normalismo has never let up.

🇲🇽⚖️ <u>Mexico's elected Supreme Court turns one</u>

One year ago Mexico did what no country had dared: it chose its Supreme Court justices by popular vote. Today the renewed judiciary marks its first anniversary, with President Sheinbaum in attendance and Chief Justice Hugo Aguilar Ortiz — the first Indigenous person to lead the Court — presenting the balance. The 2024 reform closed the door on a judicial caste that for decades shielded the powerful; the bench elected on Sept. 1 now answers to the voters who put it there.
